items.pronunciation_notes: म loses its vertical stem and प follows. Modern Hindi increasingly writes this cluster with the anusvara instead, as ंप, and both spellings are read the same way.

learn.title_en: म्प — the stack that is losing ground
learn.explanation_en: म्प is a half-form like स्त: म drops its stem and प follows immediately. What makes it worth a card of its own is that modern Hindi is quietly replacing it. Because the anusvara is read as m before a lip consonant, संपर्क and सम्पर्क are the same word, and newspapers now overwhelmingly prefer the first. You need to read both, but you will rarely need to write the stacked form.

examples.note: Usually written संपर्क today; the two are identical in sound.
Formal vocabulary, common on newspaper mastheads.
Borrowed from English and heard on the street constantly.

practice.prompt_en: Join these two letters into a single conjunct.
practice.question: म् + प
practice.explanation_en: म drops its vertical stem and प is written straight after it.

game.explanation_en: The stack runs m straight into p, the hook over क is read before it, and the final vowel drops: sampark.

items.pronunciation_notes: क् stacked above क. The consonant is genuinely held longer, as in English 'bookkeeper' rather than 'baker'.

learn.explanation_en: क्क is another doubled consonant, and like न्न it is held rather than merely written twice. The words it appears in are all everyday ones, so this is a good place to build the habit: pause fractionally on the k in पक्का and the word sounds right immediately. Say it as a single k and you get पका, which is a different word.

examples.note: Used constantly to mean 'definite' or 'for sure'.
Breathy ध at the front, held k in the middle.
Also the name of the city of Mecca.

common_error.why_en: A single क gives पका, meaning 'cooked' or 'ripened'. The stack holds the sound longer and means something else.

practice.prompt_en: Join these two letters into a single conjunct.
practice.question: क् + क
practice.explanation_en: क् sits above क in a vertical stack, and the sound is held for longer than a single letter.

game.explanation_en: The k is held, neither k is aspirated, and the final vowel is long: pakkaa.

items.pronunciation_notes: च् stacked above च, both unaspirated. Distinguish it from च्छ, where the second letter carries a puff of breath.

learn.title_en: च्च — and how it differs from अच्छा
learn.explanation_en: च्च is a held ch with no breath on either half. It is worth setting beside अच्छा, which looks similar but is च् plus छ — the second half there is aspirated. So बच्चा has two plain ch sounds while अच्छा has a plain one followed by a breathy one. Learners who cannot yet hear aspiration tend to merge the two spellings, and both words are far too common for that to go unnoticed.

examples.note: Both halves are plain, with no puff of air anywhere.
The opposite of पक्का from the last card.
Same stack again, in a word you met when stacks were introduced.

common_error.why_en: The stack is two plain ch sounds held together, not a single aspirated छ.

practice.prompt_en: Join these two letters into a single conjunct.
practice.question: च् + च
practice.explanation_en: Both halves are the plain च. Using छ as the second letter would add a puff of breath.

game.explanation_en: The ch is held and neither half carries breath, so it is bachchaa rather than bachhaa.

summary.recap_en: This level added म्प, क्क and च्च. The doubled stacks are genuinely held longer rather than just written twice, and म्प is increasingly written with the anusvara instead.
summary.next_up_en: Next: ज्ज, त्त and प्प, three more doubled stacks in very common words.

items.pronunciation_notes: ज् above ज, held longer than a single j. Neither half is aspirated.

learn.explanation_en: ज्ज follows the same pattern as क्क and च्च: the first letter stacks above the second and the sound is held. It is less frequent than the others in everyday speech and clusters in slightly formal vocabulary, but the words it appears in are ones you will read rather than words you can avoid.

examples.note: Polite and slightly formal, common in written Hindi.
Formal register; शर्म is the everyday word.
Colloquial and very common in speech.

practice.prompt_en: Join these two letters into a single conjunct.
practice.question: ज् + ज
practice.explanation_en: ज् stacks above ज, and neither half carries breath — झ as the second letter would add it.

game.explanation_en: The j is held, both vowels are short, and the final vowel drops: sajjan.

items.pronunciation_notes: त् above त, both dental. Keep the tongue on the teeth throughout — an English t here would give the retroflex ट्ट instead.

learn.title_en: त्त — held, and firmly on the teeth
learn.explanation_en: त्त combines two things you have already had to work at separately: holding a doubled consonant, and keeping the dental position that English never uses. Both halves are dental, so the tongue stays against the back of the upper teeth for the whole length of the sound. Let it drift back and you produce ट्ट, which is a different stack.

examples.note: One word for both meanings, and you will need each of them.
Held t, then a long final vowel.
Used for lamps, headlights and traffic lights alike.

practice.prompt_en: Join these two letters into a single conjunct.
practice.question: त् + त
practice.explanation_en: त् stacks above त. Using थ as the second letter would release the sound with breath.

game.explanation_en: The t is held, the first vowel is short, and the final vowel drops: uttar.

items.pronunciation_notes: प् above प, neither half aspirated. The lips stay closed slightly longer than for a single प.

learn.title_en: प्प — lips closed a little longer
learn.explanation_en: प्प holds the lips shut for an extra beat before releasing them, and crucially releases with no breath at all. That combination is awkward for English speakers, who tend to let a puff escape when they hold a p, turning the stack towards फ. Hold the closure, then open the lips quietly.

examples.note: You will hear this daily; the final vowel drops.
The stack closes the word.
Aspirated छ at the front, unaspirated held p in the middle.

practice.prompt_en: Join these two letters into a single conjunct.
practice.question: प् + प
practice.explanation_en: प् stacks above प, and neither half releases any breath — फ as the second letter would.

game.explanation_en: The p is held, both vowels are short, and the final vowel drops: chappal.

summary.recap_en: This level covered ज्ज, त्त and प्प. All three are held longer than a single letter, and त्त and प्प each combine that with something already difficult — the dental position and the absence of aspiration.
summary.next_up_en: Next: ल्ल, श्व and ष्ट complete the common stacks.

items.pronunciation_notes: ल् above ल, held longer than a single l and kept clear throughout — English darkens a long l, and Hindi does not.

learn.explanation_en: ल्ल holds the l for an extra beat. The difficulty is not the length but the quality: English darkens its l when it is held or final, so 'Delhi' said the English way has a swallowed l in the middle. Hindi keeps the sound bright and forward for its whole length. This stack appears in the name of the capital city, so it is worth getting right early.

examples.note: The l is held and stays clear; the final vowel is long.
Same shape as the city name, one letter apart.
Short vowel first, held l, then a long one.

practice.prompt_en: Join these two letters into a single conjunct.
practice.question: ल् + ल
practice.explanation_en: ल् stacks above ल, giving one held sound rather than two separate syllables.

game.explanation_en: The first vowel is short, the l is held, and the final vowel is the long ी: dillii.

items.pronunciation_notes: श् plus व as a half-form. The व keeps its light contact — the lips approach the teeth without meeting.

learn.explanation_en: श्व is a half-form: श loses its stem and व follows. The pair is awkward for English speakers because there is no vowel to lean on between the two sounds, and the temptation is to insert one and say 'vish-uh-vaas'. Run them together. Note also that this cluster drops its final vowel — विश्व is 'vishv' — which is the pattern the last level of this module explains.

examples.note: Common in both speech and writing.
Seen constantly in विश्व कप, the World Cup.
Formal and literary; घोड़ा is the everyday word.

practice.prompt_en: Join these two letters into a single conjunct.
practice.question: श् + व
practice.explanation_en: श drops its stem and व follows immediately, with no vowel between the two.

game.explanation_en: No vowel comes between the sh and the v, and only the last syllable is long: vishvaas.

items.pronunciation_notes: ष plus the retroflex ट. ष is pronounced like श today, so the cluster is 'sht' with the tongue curled back for the t.

learn.title_en: ष्ट — and a preview of the next level
learn.explanation_en: ष्ट pairs the retroflex sibilant with the retroflex ट. Since ष and श sound identical today, the cluster is simply 'sht', with the tongue curled back for the second half. Look closely at राष्ट्र below: the same cluster with र added, and unlike कष्ट it keeps its final vowel. That difference is the subject of the next level.

examples.note: The final vowel drops, so the word ends on the cluster.
Same pattern; common in news writing.
Here र is added and the final vowel is pronounced.

practice.prompt_en: Join these two letters into a single conjunct.
practice.question: ष् + ट
practice.explanation_en: ष loses its stem and the retroflex ट follows, with no breath released and no vowel between.

game.explanation_en: No vowel comes between the sh and the retroflex t, and the final vowel drops: kashṭ.

summary.recap_en: This level finished the common stacks with ल्ल, श्व and ष्ट. Two of them, विश्व and कष्ट, drop their final vowel while राष्ट्र keeps its own — the question the next level answers.
summary.next_up_en: Next: which written vowels are actually pronounced — the rule that decides how every Hindi word ends.

items.pronunciation_notes: The inherent अ at the end of a word is not pronounced in modern standard Hindi. कमल is kamal, नमक is namak, घर is ghar.

learn.title_en: The final अ is not pronounced
learn.explanation_en: Every consonant carries an inherent अ, but the one at the end of a word is dropped. This is near-categorical in modern standard Hindi, so treat it as a firm rule rather than a tendency: कमल is 'kamal', नमक is 'namak', घर is 'ghar'. English speakers who sound out every letter produce 'kamala' and 'namaka', which is how Sanskrit is recited rather than how Hindi is spoken. There are two named exceptions, and the next card covers them.

examples.note: Three letters, two syllables — the last vowel is written but silent.
Ask for 'namaka' and you will be understood, but you will sound like a textbook.
One syllable, not two.

common_error.why_en: Writing the ा matra makes the final vowel real: कमला is a woman's name, while कमल is the flower.

practice.prompt_en: Build the word 'namak' from these letters.
practice.question: न + म + क
practice.explanation_en: All three letters carry an inherent vowel in writing, but the last one is not pronounced: namak.

game.explanation_en: The final vowel is written but silent, and neither of the other two is long: kamal.

items.pronunciation_notes: The final vowel survives after a conjunct ending in र or य, and in Sanskrit words recited in a devotional register. Conjuncts ending in a stop or a nasal drop it as usual.
items.gloss_en: when the final schwa is kept

learn.title_en: Two places the final अ survives
learn.explanation_en: The rule has two named exceptions. First, a word ending in a conjunct can keep its vowel — but only some conjuncts do, so 'after a conjunct' is too loose. मित्र is 'mitra' and राष्ट्र is 'raashṭra' because those clusters end in र, and सत्य is 'satya' because it ends in य. Clusters ending in a stop or a nasal follow the ordinary rule, which is why शुद्ध is 'shuddh', अन्न is 'ann' and कष्ट is 'kashṭ'. Second, Sanskrit words recited devotionally keep the vowel: कृष्ण is 'krishn' in ordinary speech but 'krishna' when chanted.

examples.note: The cluster ends in र, so the vowel is heard.
The same cluster from the last level, now with र, and now with a final vowel.
This cluster ends in a stop, so the ordinary rule applies and the vowel drops.

common_error.why_en: Not every conjunct keeps the final vowel. This one ends in a stop, so it behaves like any ordinary word ending.

practice.prompt_en: Build the word 'mitra' from these letters.
practice.question: म + ि + त् + र
practice.explanation_en: The final vowel is pronounced without any matra being written, because the conjunct ends in र.

game.explanation_en: The cluster ends in र, so the final vowel survives: raashṭra rather than raashṭr.

items.pronunciation_notes: Medial schwa deletion is variable and depends on the word's structure. नमस्ते keeps its middle vowel while समझ drops its final one, and no single rule covers every case.

learn.explanation_en: Inside a word the inherent अ sometimes drops and sometimes does not, and unlike the word-final rule this one has no exceptionless form — so do not try to learn it as one. A useful pattern rather than a rule: the vowel tends to go when removing it still leaves something pronounceable, and tends to stay when it does not. Compare समझ, said 'samajh' with its middle vowel intact, against समझना, where adding an ending makes that same vowel disappear. Even native speakers vary, so learn these word by word.

examples.note: Two syllables — the middle vowel stays and the final one goes.
The same word plus an ending, and now a vowel drops inside it.
Every written vowel here is pronounced.

practice.prompt_en: Build the word 'samajh' from these letters.
practice.question: स + म + झ
practice.explanation_en: The middle vowel is pronounced and the final one is not, giving two syllables: samajh.

game.explanation_en: The first two vowels are both pronounced here, unlike the pattern in समझना: namaste.

summary.recap_en: This level established the rule that governs how every Hindi word ends: the final inherent अ is dropped. It survives only after a conjunct ending in र or य, and in devotional recitation. Inside a word the same vowel behaves variably and has to be learned word by word.
summary.next_up_en: Module 4 leaves the script behind and begins vocabulary, starting with family words and the gender that every Hindi noun carries.
